---
title: "The Chinese restaurant process"
subtitle: "Catalog P-07 · after Broderick (MLSS 2016, part II)"
description: "Units arrive one at a time and join existing clusters in proportion to their size, or open a new one in proportion to alpha."
toc: false
---

Imagine the J units of a study (sites, schools, studies) arriving one at a time at a
restaurant with infinitely many tables. The first sits at table 1. Unit n + 1 joins an
occupied table k with probability n_k / (alpha + n), where n_k is the number already
there, and opens a new table with probability alpha / (alpha + n). Large tables attract
more newcomers ("the rich get richer"), and alpha works like a pseudo-count for the
tables nobody has sat at yet.

```{=html}

<script src="../../js/vendor/d3.min.js"></script>

</script>
```

## What to try

- **alpha = 1, Seat 1 eight times.** The factor strip below the bar reproduces
  Broderick's example: the probability of a seating is the product of one factor per
  arrival, alpha/alpha for the first, then n_k/(alpha + n) or alpha/(alpha + n).
- **Seat 100 at alpha = 0.01, then at alpha = 2.** With a tiny alpha nearly everyone
  ends up at one table; with alpha = 2 a handful of tables share the room.
- **The STAR read-out.** With J = 79 schools, the 79th school opens a new cluster with
  probability alpha/(alpha + 78): 1.3% at alpha = 1 and 6.0% at alpha = 5. By then the
  expected number of clusters is E(K_79 | alpha) = Σ alpha/(alpha + i − 1).
- **Say sites and clusters** relabels the picture in the language of a multisite study.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
After Broderick (MLSS 2016, Cádiz, part II; 2012 tutorial); re-implemented from the
mathematics. The seating is seeded, so the same seed and alpha reproduce the same
restaurant. Keyboard: Tab to the controls; Enter seats one more.
:::

Standalone version: [embed/crp.html](../../embed/crp.html) (for example `?alpha=0.5`).

## How K_N grows (P-08)

Follow the number of occupied tables K_N as customers keep arriving. Its expectation
E[K_N] = Σ alpha/(alpha + n − 1) grows like alpha log N: slowly, but without bound. At a
fixed N, the exact distribution of K_N is the Antoniak distribution, which is exactly
what the rest of the site calls the prior of K_J for a study with J = N units.

```{=html}
<div id="w-growth" class="dpx-host column-page"></div>
<script src="../../js/bundles/crp-growth.js"></script>
<script>
  window.__dpxGrowth = DPX["crp-growth"].mountWidget(document.getElementById("w-growth"), { alpha: 1, N: 100 });
</script>
```

At alpha = 1 and N = 100, E[K_100] = 5.19: the average of the black curve and the mean of
the bars in panel B are the same number. Add 1000 customers and switch the N axis to log:
the staircase follows alpha log N. The dotted guides mark N = 48, 79 and 500, the sizes of
the paper's three applications.
